data.title: Reverse Bits
data.summary:
Input: An integer n representing a 32-bit unsigned integer.
Output: An integer representing the number formed by reversing the 32 bits of n.
Rules: Treat n as a 32-bit unsigned quantity.
constraints: The input must be a binary string of length 32 or a 32-bit integer.

data.generator_code:
import random
def generate(rng, n):
    val = rng.getrandbits(32)
    return [val]
def generate_worst(rng, n):
    val = rng.getrandbits(32)
    return [val]

data.key_insight: We can construct the reversed integer bit by bit. By iterating 32 times, we extract the least significant bit of the input, shift our result to the left to make room, and add the extracted bit.

steps.title: Initialize Result
steps.detail: Create a variable `reversed_bits` set to 0 to store the final reversed binary representation.

steps.title: Iterate 32 Times
steps.detail: Loop 32 times, once for each bit of the 32-bit unsigned integer.

steps.title: Shift and Extract
steps.detail: Shift `reversed_bits` left by 1 to make space for the next bit, then add the least significant bit of `n` (obtained via `n & 1`).

steps.title: Shift Input Right
steps.detail: Shift `n` right by 1 to process the next bit in the subsequent iteration.

data.pattern_summary: Bit manipulation involves using bitwise operators like AND, OR, and shifts to directly inspect and modify individual bits of numbers, useful when dealing with fixed-size binary representations.

pattern_options.name: Bit Manipulation
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. The problem asks us to reverse the bits of a fixed 32-bit integer, which requires processing individual bits using shifts and masks.

pattern_options.name: Sliding Window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding windows are used for contiguous subarrays or substrings, not for rearranging bits of a number.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. DP is used for overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure, which is unnecessary here.

pattern_options.name: Two Pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers traverse linear data structures from different ends, which does not match bit-level operations.

signals.hint: Implies we must operate at the individual bit level rather than the whole number level.
Tells us the exact fixed size of the input, meaning our operation count will always be bounded by 32.

data.brute_force_idea: Loop 32 times. In each iteration, extract the last bit of n, shift the result to the left, add the extracted bit, and right-shift n.
data.brute_force_why: The loop runs a fixed number of 32 iterations regardless of the input value, meaning it takes constant time.
data.bottleneck: There is no wasted work. A 32-bit integer always requires checking all 32 positions, so processing each bit once is already the theoretical limit of efficiency.
bottleneck_hints: Count how many bits a 32-bit integer has.
Ask yourself if you can skip looking at any of the 32 bits and still know what to reverse.
Recognize that since the input size is strictly fixed at 32 operations, the time complexity is already O(1) constant time.

data.overview: This algorithm reverses the bits of a 32-bit integer by iterating through each bit position. It extracts the least significant bit of the input and shifts it into the corresponding position in the result.
data.intuition: Imagine a conveyor belt where you pick items one by one from the end of one line and place them at the front of a new line, effectively reversing the order.

flow_nodes.detail: We start with an empty 32-bit container.

flow_nodes.label: Loop 32 times
flow_nodes.detail: We must process every single bit of the 32-bit integer.

flow_nodes.label: Shift result left
flow_nodes.detail: Make space for the new bit by shifting current bits left.

flow_nodes.label: Add LSB of n
flow_nodes.detail: Extract the last bit of n and place it into the result.

flow_nodes.label: Shift n right
flow_nodes.detail: Discard the bit just processed from n.

flow_nodes.label: Return result
flow_nodes.detail: The fully constructed reversed integer is returned.

pitfalls: Forgetting to treat the number as a 32-bit unsigned integer.
Shifting the result before adding the new bit, leading to incorrect bit placement.
Using a loop that does not run exactly 32 times.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The optimized solution removes the overhead of string conversions and slicing by directly processing the integer at the bit level. It loops exactly 32 times regardless of the input value because the bit-width is fixed by definition. This constant number of operations keeps both time and memory consumption strictly bounded.

derivation.note: The loop header runs 32 times plus 1 final check to terminate.
Bitwise shift and OR operations execute once per iteration.
Right shift of n executes once per iteration.

data.time_summary: Lines 4, 5, and 6 run a constant 32 times based on the fixed 32-bit integer size, meaning the step count stays fixed at 99 steps even as the input size grows. Therefore, the time complexity is O(1).
data.space_summary: Only a few scalar integer variables (reversed_bits, n) are maintained in memory, requiring O(1) space.
data.takeaway: When dealing with fixed-size primitives like 32-bit integers, bit manipulation loops bounded by the fixed bit-width yield O(1) time and space complexity.
mistakes: Treating the input as a variable-length string instead of a fixed 32-bit integer.
Forgetting to apply unsigned right shift logic or mismanaging bit precedence in expressions like (res << 1) | (n & 1).
